# Bidirekt

> Bidirekt is a static, bidirectional contract testing tool. Each participant (provider or consumer) writes a YAML contract declaring what it provides and what it consumes, publishes it to a broker with the `bidirekt` CLI, and asks `can-i-deploy` before deploying. Nothing is run: the broker compares declarations.

Workflow per participant, in this order: `create-participant` (once) → `validate` (before commit) → `publish` (every build) → `can-i-deploy` (before deploy) → deploy → `record-deployment` (after deploy succeeds).

## Setup

Install the CLI (Linux and macOS, `x86_64` and `arm64`):

```
curl -sSfL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/bidirekt/cli/main/install.sh | sh
```

Point it at your broker, once per machine. `bidirekt configure` asks for the URL; `bidirekt configure --broker-url <url>` never asks:

```
bidirekt configure
bidirekt configure --broker-url <url>
```

Install the agent skill that writes and fixes the contract files from the code:

```
npx skills add bidirekt/skills
```

## Contract file

YAML, extension `.yaml` or `.yml`, one document per file. Three optional top-level keys, nothing else: `provides`, `consumes`, `schemas`. Participant name and version are CLI flags, never keys in the file. One file may carry both `provides` and `consumes`.

```yaml
# provider petstore_api
provides:
  rest:
    /pets/*:
      get:
        responses:
          200: Pet
    /pets:
      post:
        request: NewPet
        responses:
          201: Pet
          400: Error

# consumer petstore_web: same rest block, nested under the provider's participant name
consumes:
  petstore_api:
    rest:
      /pets/*:
        get:
          responses:
            200: Pet

schemas:
  Pet:
    type: object
    properties:
      petId:
        type: integer
      name:
        type: string
      nickname:
        type: string
        optional: true
  Pets:
    type: array
    items:
      ref: Pet
```

Rules:

- Resource = one body: the request of (endpoint, method), or one response of (endpoint, method, status). Each is compared on its own.
- Methods: `get`, `post`, `put`, `patch`, `delete`, lowercase only. `request` only on `post`, `put` and `patch`. A method may have only `request`, only `responses`, or both.
- `request` and each status in `responses` name a schema declared under `schemas`, or are `~` (or no value, `204:`) = body not described: nothing in it is compared, the resource still exists. Never an inline schema. `""` is an unresolved schema name, not `~`. Provider `200: ~` vs consumer `200: Pet` breaks once, on the body; provider `200: Pet` vs consumer `200: ~` and provider `request: ~` vs consumer `request: NewFile` are compatible.
- Status: integer 100–599, quoted or not. No patterns (`2xx` rejected).
- Endpoint: starts with `/`, no empty segment. Dynamic segment = `*`, one per segment, unnamed (`/owners/*/pets/*`). `{petId}` and `p*` are rejected; `:petId` is a literal segment that matches nothing. Trailing slash is removed (`/pets/` = `/pets`). Consumer and provider endpoints match only when written identically.
- Consumer key under `consumes` = the provider's participant name, snake_case. Not checked at publish: a typo publishes and fails at `can-i-deploy` with "doesn't provide it".
- Schema node `type`: `object`, `array`, `string`, `integer`, `float`, `number`, `boolean`. No enums, no formats. `integer` ≠ `float`, both strict. A `number` reader accepts an `integer`, `float` or `number` producer; a `number` producer breaks an `integer` or `float` reader (JSON sends `50` for a round float: read it as `number`).
- `object` takes `properties`, `values` or neither; `array` needs `items`. `type` may be omitted when `properties`, `values` or `items` is present.
- `{type: object}` with neither `properties` nor `values` = any object, for an object the code does not read inside (`metadata: {type: object}` passed along as it came; `items: {type: object}` for items only counted). As reader it accepts any object, nothing inside is compared; as producer it declares no property, so each property the reader requires directly in it breaks (`doesn't provide`; `doesn't send` in a request).
- Map (dynamic keys, all values one shape): `values: <node>` instead of `properties`, e.g. `PetsByName: {type: object, values: {ref: Pet}}` for `{"bob": {...}, "sky": {...}}`. Keys are strings. `values` with `properties` → `object schema has both "values" and "properties"`; `values` with a non-object `type` → `"values" on a non-object schema`. Values compare like array items; the key is the path segment `{}` (`$.pets{}.name`), the type prints `map<T>`. A map reader accepts fixed properties from the producer: each is compared against `values` (type, `nullable`, members) and breaks at its own property (`$.pets.sky`); its `optional` never breaks (a map requires no key). Still breaking: a fixed-property reader against a map producer (`$.pets.bob` against `$.pets{}` breaks with `doesn't provide`), and a `{type: object}` producer with no properties against a map reader (breaks at `$.pets{}`).
- Properties are required unless `optional: true` (the key may be missing). There is no `required` list. `nullable: true` (any node: property, `items`, `values`, root) = the key is there and the value may be `null`; independent of `optional`.
- Modeling null and absence: write what the code does, not the type it declares (a nullable type the code never sets to `null` gets no `nullable`). The reader writes the flags from how its code reads each property, the producer from what its code can send (response: consumer reads, provider produces; request: the reverse):
  | The code | Write |
  |---|---|
  | reads the property with no fallback (`pet.name`, `as String`) | neither `optional` nor `nullable` |
  | accepts `null` but needs the key (`pet.nickname === null ? … : …`) | `nullable: true` |
  | accepts a missing key but not `null` | `optional: true` |
  | accepts both (`??`, `?.` in JS; `as T?` in Dart) | `optional: true` and `nullable: true` |
  | produces the body and may send `null` for the property | `nullable: true` |
  | produces the body and may leave the key out | `optional: true` |
- `ref: <SchemaName>` reuses a named schema at any depth; allowed beside it: only `optional`, `nullable`, `description` (either one makes the node optional/nullable even when the named schema is not). If the node also has `type`/`properties`/`items`/`values`, the `ref` is silently ignored. Unknown `ref` is rejected.
- Recursion is allowed: a schema may `ref` itself directly or indirectly (`Comment.replies[] → Comment`, `Post.author → User` / `User.posts[] → Post`). No depth limit.
- `description` is allowed on any node and ignored.
- Every unknown key at any level is a violation (`options`, `GET`, top-level `version`). YAML anchors/aliases are rejected; comments are allowed.
- Declare only what you use: a consumer lists only the properties it reads or sends; the provider may drop anything else.

Several files: all files of one `publish` are one contract, order irrelevant.

- Schema names are one namespace across files; the same name twice is a duplicate.
- Provider: each resource declared in exactly one file (endpoints, methods or statuses may be split across files, but the `request` of an endpoint+method lives in one file only). A file reached twice (passed twice, or passed and also inside a passed folder) is read once, not a duplicate.
- Consumer: fragments of the same resource merge. Response: a property is optional only if every fragment marks it optional, nullable only if every fragment marks it nullable. Request: required only if every fragment sends it (a fragment that lacks its parent too doesn't count), nullable if any fragment marks it nullable. Different types for one property are rejected.

Not compared (never breaks): headers, query parameters, enum values, string formats.

## CLI

Every broker command needs a broker URL; there is no default. Resolution: `--broker-url` → `BIDIREKT_BROKER_URL` → the active profile's saved URL. Active profile: `--profile` → `BIDIREKT_PROFILE` → `default`. With none: `no broker configured — pass --broker-url, set BIDIREKT_BROKER_URL, or run "bidirekt configure"`. Global flags go before or after the command. In CI, use `BIDIREKT_BROKER_URL`.

- `bidirekt configure [--profile <name>] [--broker-url <url>]` — saves the URL in `~/.config/bidirekt/config.json` (or `$XDG_CONFIG_HOME/bidirekt/config.json`, or `BIDIREKT_CONFIG_FILE`). Without `--broker-url` it prompts; outside a terminal it fails. URL must be `http://` or `https://` plus a host. One profile per broker (account), never per environment.
- `bidirekt create-participant <name>` — name in snake_case (`participant name must be snake_case`). Idempotent: `already exists` exits 0.
- `bidirekt create-environment <name>` — e.g. `production`. Idempotent.
- `bidirekt validate <file or folder>... --participant <name> --environment <env>` — reads files and folders and checks them as `publish` does, then compares them with every counterpart deployed in `<env>`, as `can-i-deploy` does. Nothing is stored. Exit 0 = yes, exit 1 = no; the report goes to stdout either way, starts with `<participant> local contract can be deployed to <env>` or `<participant> local contract cannot be deployed to <env>`, and carries the same break lines as `can-i-deploy` (see `## Fixing can-i-deploy breaks`). Violations print as in `publish`. Participant and environment are checked before any file: `participant "<name>" not found → create it with: bidirekt create-participant <name>`, `environment not found`.
- `bidirekt publish <file or folder>... --participant <name> --version <label>` — all files publish together as one contract. A folder = every `.yaml`/`.yml` file under it, subfolders included, other files ignored; a folder with none fails with `no contract YAML files in folder: "<folder>"`. Files and folders mix in one command; the files go in alphabetical order, and a file reached twice is read once, named as the first argument that reached it. A file found in a folder is named by the folder plus its path inside it, without a leading `./` (`./contracts/` → `contracts/rest/pets.yaml`); a file passed directly keeps its name as typed. Participant must exist, checked before any file (`participant "<name>" not found → create it with: bidirekt create-participant <name>`). Same version with different content fails (`contract version already exists with different content`); versions are immutable. Any spec violation rejects the whole publish and prints every violation:
  ```
  contract validation failed
    - petstore_api.yaml: invalid endpoint "/pets/{petId}" at provides rest, dynamic path segments must use *
  ```
- `bidirekt can-i-deploy <participant> --version <v> --environment <env>` — exit 0 = yes, exit 1 = no; the report goes to stdout either way. Errors: `contract not found` (version never published), `environment not found`, `participant not found`.
- `bidirekt record-deployment <participant> --version <v> --environment <env>` — run after a successful deploy. Never blocks. Prints `<participant> deployment recorded to <env>`. Recording a version that was deployed in `<env>` before and is not the current one there is a rollback, and prints `<participant> rolled back to <version> in <env>`.
- `bidirekt rename-participant <old> <new>` — not idempotent (`participant already exists`). Renaming a provider is a migration: rename → publish and deploy the provider → switch every consumer's `consumes` key.
- `bidirekt list-participants` — prints every participant name, one per line on stdout, in alphabetical order; nothing when there are none, exit 0. Check names here before writing `consumes`.
- `bidirekt list-environments` — prints every environment name, one per line on stdout, in alphabetical order; nothing when there are none, exit 0. Check names here before passing `--environment`.
- `bidirekt version` (or `--version`, `-v`).

Exit codes: 0 on success, help and version; 1 for everything else. Success goes to stdout, failures to stderr, except the `can-i-deploy` and `validate` reports (always stdout).

## Fixing can-i-deploy breaks

Report shape: `<participant> <version> cannot be deployed to <env>`, then one block per incompatible counterpart → endpoint → `request` / `response <status>` → one break per line, each followed by its fix lines; a removed endpoint's break prints once, right below `<METHOD> <endpoint>`, outside any `request` / `response <status>` group. `<property>` is a path from the body root: `$.owner.name`, `$[].photoUrl` (array items), `$.pets{}.name` (map values); the root prints as `the body`, unquoted. Types print `array<T>` and `map<T>`. Right after it, in parentheses, comes `<f>`, the field of the participant under check: schema name + path inside that schema (`Address.city`, `Pet.vaccinations[].name` for array items, `Pets{}.name` for map values, only `Pet` at the root). That is the schema to edit in its contract. No parentheses when that participant has no field there (the `doesn't provide` and `doesn't send` lines). A difference inside a schema used in several places is reported once per resource (once under each request and each response status), with one of the paths that reach it:
  ```
  - petstore_web reads "$.owner.address.city" (Address.city), but petstore_api doesn't provide it
    → petstore_web: stop reading it, or handle its absence in the code and mark it optional
    → petstore_api: provide it
  - petstore_web reads the body (Pet) as object, but petstore_api provides array<object>
    → petstore_web: read it as array<object>
    → petstore_api: provide it as object at Pets
  ```
Below each break come its fixes, one line per side, the participant under check first: `→ <participant>: <fix>`, then `→ <c>: <fix>`, which ends with ` at <cf>` (the counterpart's own field) when the counterpart has one there. A fix is a code change first, then the contract change that matches it: the contract follows the code. When `<p>` ends with `[]` or `{}` (array items, map values), the reading side's fix that would mark it optional reads the parent instead, `read "<parent>" the way <producer> provides it` (in a request, `sends it`), with no ` at`. Each break, with the fix of the participant under check, then `<c>`'s:

- `reads "<p>" (<f>), but <c> doesn't provide it` → `stop reading it, or handle its absence in the code and mark it optional`; <c>: `provide it`.
- `doesn't provide "<p>", but <c> reads it` → `provide it`; <c>: `stop reading it, or handle its absence in the code and mark it optional at <cf>`.
- `requires "<p>" (<f>), but <c> only sometimes provides it` → `handle its absence in the code, then mark it optional`; <c>: `always provide it at <cf>`.
- `provides "<p>" (<f>) only sometimes, but <c> requires it` → `always provide it`; <c>: `handle its absence in the code, then mark it optional at <cf>`.
- `doesn't send "<p>", but <c> requires it` → `send it`; <c>: `stop requiring it, then mark it optional at <cf>`.
- `requires "<p>" (<f>), but <c> doesn't send it` → `stop requiring it, then mark it optional`; <c>: `send it`.
- `sends "<p>" (<f>) only sometimes, but <c> requires it` → `always send it`; <c>: `handle its absence in the code, then mark it optional at <cf>`.
- `requires "<p>" (<f>), but <c> sends it only sometimes` → `handle its absence in the code, then mark it optional`; <c>: `always send it at <cf>`.
- `reads "<p>" (<f>) as <t>, but <c> provides <t2>` → `read it as <t2>`; <c>: `provide it as <t> at <cf>`.
- `provides "<p>" (<f>) as <t>, but <c> reads <t2>` → `provide it as <t2>`; <c>: `read it as <t> at <cf>`.
- `sends "<p>" (<f>) as <t>, but <c> expects <t2>` → `send <t2>`; <c>: `accept <t> at <cf>`.
- `expects "<p>" (<f>) as <t>, but <c> sends <t2>` → `accept <t2>`; <c>: `send <t> at <cf>`.
- `doesn't accept null at "<p>" (<f>), but <c> may provide null` → `handle null in the code, then mark it nullable`; <c>: `stop providing null at <cf>`.
- `may provide null at "<p>" (<f>), but <c> doesn't accept it` → `stop providing null`; <c>: `handle null in the code, then mark it nullable at <cf>`.
- `may send null at "<p>" (<f>), but <c> doesn't accept it` → `stop sending null`; <c>: `handle null in the code, then mark it nullable at <cf>`.
- `doesn't accept null at "<p>" (<f>), but <c> may send it` → `handle null in the code, then mark it nullable`; <c>: `stop sending null at <cf>`.
- `calls <METHOD> <endpoint>, but <c> doesn't provide it` → `stop calling it`; <c>: `publish it`. Check endpoint spelling (`*` segments), method, status and the provider name under `consumes`.
- `calls <METHOD> <endpoint>, but <c> is not deployed in <env>` (plus ` (deployed in: <envs>)` when it is deployed elsewhere) → only <c>: `deploy it to <env> first`.
- `removed <METHOD> <endpoint>, but <c> still calls it` → `keep it until <c> stops calling it`; <c>: `stop calling it`. Printed once, right below `<METHOD> <endpoint>`, not under each body.

Core rule: the side that reads a body decides what must be in it. Response: provider produces, consumer reads. Request: consumer produces, provider reads. A property the reader requires must be declared by the producer, required too, with a type the reader accepts (the same type; a `number` reader also accepts `integer` and `float`). A property is required only where its parent is present: when the producer does not declare a parent, only the parent can break, nothing inside it is checked (array items and map values included). A property the reader marks optional may be absent, but if both declare it the reader must accept its type. A property the producer marks nullable must be nullable for the reader too. A property the reader does not declare is not checked.
